prompt: Which statement about look-ahead bias is correct?

options.text: Look-ahead only affects fundamental data such as company accounts.
A decision uses information that did not exist at the time of the decision.
Statistics computed once on all the data are harmless.
A same-close fill is fine if the entry is at the same close.

explanations.a: Look-ahead can enter through price data, such as a same-close fill or a full-sample statistic, not only through company accounts.
explanations.c: A statistic computed once on all the data can use years after the signal. That is a leak.
explanations.d: The close was not known until the day ended. A fill at that close is not realistic.

prompt: A rule sees a signal at today's close of Rs 300. Which fill is realistic?

options.text: Rs 300 at the same close, since the signal came from that close.
Rs 303 at the next open, since the close was only known after the market shut.
The low of the signal day, since that is the best price.
Any price from the signal day, as long as it is in the data.

explanations.a: This is a same-close fill. The close was not known until the day ended, so the fill is not realistic.
explanations.c: The low of the signal day was reached before the decision could be made. It is not a realistic fill either.
explanations.d: Being in the data does not make a price tradable at the time of the decision. The fill must come after the signal.

prompt: Hypothetical. The peek run fills at Rs 300 and the honest run fills at Rs 303. On 10 shares, how many rupees more does the honest run cost per trade?
solution: Honest cost = 10 x 303 = Rs 3,030. Peek cost = 10 x 300 = Rs 3,000. Difference = 3,030 - 3,000 = Rs 30. Check: 3 rupees a share x 10 shares = Rs 30.

prompt: Hypothetical. The peek run shows a profit of Rs 12,000 and the honest run shows Rs 8,000 on the same rules. What does the gap suggest?

options.text: The honest run is wrong, because it is lower.
The rules may leak information, so the peek result overstates what the rules could have made.
Look-ahead makes results lower, so the peek run is the pessimistic one.
Both runs are equally honest, and the gap is just noise.

explanations.a: The honest run is the one you could have traded. A lower result is not a sign of error.
explanations.c: Look-ahead makes results look better, not worse. The peek run is the optimistic one.
explanations.d: A gap of this size on the same rules points to a leak. It should be found and explained, not called noise.

prompt: Here is a rule: Enter today if tomorrow's high is above Rs 310. Which part is wrong?

options.text: Entering today, which is always allowed.
Using tomorrow's high to decide today, because tomorrow's high is not known when today's decision is made.
The threshold of Rs 310, which is too low.
Nothing is wrong, because the high is part of the data.

explanations.a: Entering today is not the problem. The decision uses a value from tomorrow, which is the leak.
explanations.c: The size of the threshold does not matter here. Any threshold on tomorrow's high leaks information.
explanations.d: Being in the data does not make a value known at the time of the decision.

prompt: A rule ranks today's close against the median close of all years in the data. Which part is wrong?

options.text: Nothing is wrong, because a median is always harmless.
The median includes years after the signal, so it uses future information.
The median is too slow to calculate.
It is only a problem for adjusted data.

explanations.a: A median over all years is a full-sample statistic. It is a common source of look-ahead.
explanations.c: Speed is not the issue. The issue is which data the number can see on the day.
explanations.d: This is a leak in any price data, adjusted or not, when the statistic uses future years.
